Monday, 7 June. Atelier Rhône. Nathalie, the boss, has called Ioana and Karim into the meeting room. On the table there’s a big envelope from the Lyon city council.
Sit down. I have some important news. Do you remember the competition for the renovation of the care home in Fourvière?
Of course. We worked on it all winter. But as there were twelve architecture firms, I didn’t really believe in it.
(she smiles) Well, you were wrong. We won!
Really? But… why us? There were firms much bigger than ours.
Thanks to you, Ioana. The jury loved your idea of a music room on the ground floor, opening onto the garden. They said it was the only project designed for the residents, and not just for the walls.
That makes sense, since she goes there every week with Julien! She knows the building better than anyone.
Exactly. That’s why I’ve decided you’ll lead the project, Ioana. It’s your first project as project manager.
(moved) Me? But I’ve only been here two years…
And you’re the best architect in the studio. Don’t tell Karim.
I’m sitting right next to you, Nathalie… (he laughs) But she’s right. Is there a problem, though?
Yes, the budget. Because of the crisis, the city has cut the budget by fifteen per cent. So we’ll have to make choices.
We don’t touch the music room. The residents have almost nothing to entertain themselves, so many of them stay in their rooms all day.
All right. Then we’ll save elsewhere. The building work starts in September and will last a year, because the residents have to stay on site during the work.
I’ll tell Hélène on Wednesday. She’ll be delighted, because the music room was partly her idea too.

1. Cause: parce que, comme, puisque, car
They all express cause, but with different nuances:
new cause, after the fact; answers “pourquoi ?”
Elle est ravie parce que c’était son idée.
cause at the START of the sentence
Comme tu connais le bâtiment, tu dirigeras le projet.
Le chantier durera un an, car…

“Comme” meaning “as/since” ALWAYS goes at the start of the sentence. “Parce que” goes after the fact. In careful writing you don’t say “Parce que tu connais le bâtiment, tu…”; you say “Comme tu connais…”.
2. Grâce à and à cause de
Both are followed by a NOUN or a PRONOUN (not a verb). The difference is emotional:
Nous avons gagné grâce à toi.
Le budget a baissé à cause de la crise.
The budget went down because of the crisis.
Watch the contractions: “à cause du budget” (de + le), “grâce aux résidents” (à + les), “à cause des travaux” (de + les).
As in English: “thanks to” is for good things, “because of” for bad things. You wouldn’t say “thanks to the crisis, we lost”, nor “grâce à la crise”.
3. Consequence: donc, alors, c’est pourquoi, si bien que
The budget went down, so we’ll have to make choices.
It was raining, so we stayed at home.
She knows the building. That’s why she’ll lead the project.
They have nothing to do, so they stay in their rooms.
“Alors” is the most common in speech. “Donc” is logical, like “therefore”. “C’est pourquoi” and “si bien que” are more elegant, good for writing.
Parce que le métro était en panne.
Pourquoi le projet est en retard ?
Donc / Alors nous avons décidé de…
To “Pourquoi ?” you answer “Parce que…”, not “Car…” or “Comme…”.

On Wednesday, Ioana went up to Fourvière with Julien. In her bag she had the project plans, rolled up in a big tube. As she was nervous, she had checked them three times on the metro.

Hélène was waiting for them in the common room, in front of the old piano. When Ioana unrolled the plans on the table, several residents came over. Monsieur Petit, a former postman of ninety, put on his glasses. Madame Lambert, who had been a primary school teacher, asked what they were.
“It’s your new home,” Ioana explained. “Well, the same home, but more beautiful, brighter and more practical. The work will start in September.”

She showed them every room: the bedrooms, which would have bigger windows thanks to the new structure; the dining room, which would be quieter because the street noise would be insulated; and above all, on the ground floor, a big round room, entirely glazed, opening onto the garden.

“And what’s that?” asked Monsieur Petit. “It’s the music room,” answered Ioana. “There’ll be a piano, comfortable armchairs and concerts every week. Julien has promised to come and play, and his pupils too.”

Madame Lambert applauded. Monsieur Petit said he hadn’t heard live music for twenty years, because he couldn’t go out any more because of his legs. Another lady asked if they’d be able to dance too. Ioana answered yes, of course, since the floor would be wooden.
All this time, Hélène hadn’t said anything. She was looking at the plans in silence. Ioana was starting to worry: maybe she didn’t like the project? Maybe she was afraid of the building work?
At last Hélène looked up. “Ioana, this room… does it have a name?” Ioana was surprised by the question. “No, not yet. On the plans it’s just called ‘multi-purpose room’. Why?”
Hélène smiled. “Because I have an idea. But first I need to talk to someone about it. Could Madame Bernard come on Sunday?”

On Sunday, the two ladies shut themselves in Hélène’s room for an hour. Ioana and Julien waited in the garden, like two children outside the head teacher’s office. When they came out, they were arm in arm and smiling.

“We’ve decided something,” announced Madame Bernard. “Henri was never able to play his music in public, because of his hand. But thanks to you two, his waltz was played at your wedding, in front of everyone. So we would like this room to bear his name.”
“The Henri Bernard room,” said Hélène softly. “So that a little of his music stays here, in this city he left too soon.”

Ioana had tears in her eyes. But she was also an architect, so she immediately thought of the practical problems. “It’s a wonderful idea. But I’m not the one who decides. The city does. A letter will have to be written to the Heritage Department, explaining why.”
“Well, we’ll write it together,” answered Madame Bernard. “I was a doctor for forty years. I’ve written hundreds of letters to the authorities. I know how to talk to them.”

The letter was written that very evening, in the kitchen on rue d’Austerlitz. Madame Bernard dictated, Ioana corrected the administrative phrases, Hélène added the memories, and Julien made tea. Victor, for his part, slept on the drafts.

Three weeks later, the answer arrived. Ioana opened it in front of everyone, in the common room of the care home. Her voice trembled a little. “Considering the story of Monsieur Henri Bernard, a Lyon musician, and since this request is supported by the residents… the City of Lyon agrees that the new room shall bear the name Salle Henri Bernard.”

There was a long silence. Then Monsieur Petit began to applaud, and all the residents followed. Hélène and Madame Bernard hugged each other. And Julien, without a word, sat down at the old piano and played the waltz, once again.

The following weeks were the hardest of Ioana’s working life. As she was a project manager for the first time, she wanted everything to be perfect. She came home late, ate in front of her computer, and dreamt of plans and budgets at night.

Because of the budget cut, she had to make difficult choices. There would be no new lift, only a renovation of the old one. The corridor floors wouldn’t be replaced. But the Henri Bernard room wouldn’t lose a single square metre. Ioana had fought for that through three meetings.

One evening she came home at eleven o’clock, exhausted. In the kitchen, Julien was waiting for her with a plate of pasta and a little note on the table: “Your care home will be the most beautiful in Lyon. But your husband would like to see you before it’s finished.” Ioana laughed, then she cried, then she ate the pasta.

The next day she decided to come home at seven every evening, whatever happened. And thanks to that decision, she noticed something strange: she worked better. Her ideas were clearer, her meetings shorter, and Nathalie even told her she looked happier.

On the last day before the summer holidays, Monsieur Petit gave her an envelope. Inside was a drawing made by all the residents: a big round room, full of people dancing, with a piano in the middle. At the bottom, someone had written: “Thank you, Madame Architect. Thanks to you, we feel like looking forward to the future again.”

Dear Sir or Madam, we are pleased to inform you that your project has been chosen by the competition jury.
Twelve firms took part. As the standard was very high, the choice was difficult.

Since the residents will remain in the building during the work, particular attention must be paid to noise and safety.
